title: The eruv
hook: a symbolic boundary that turns a neighborhood into one shared home for Shabbat

segments.voice: Yesterday, avot melacha, the fathers of work, and your line: work, defined. The last father on the list was carrying from one domain to another. Hold on to that one. Day one thousand seventy-three.

On some street corners, if you look up, you might spot it. Two poles, and a thin wire or string running across the top, from one pole to the next, then on down the block. You could walk under it every day and never notice. It isn't holding up a sign. It isn't carrying power. To a family on Shabbat morning, though, that wire decides whether they can push a stroller to synagogue, or carry a house key in a pocket, or bring a dish to a neighbor's lunch. Today, the string that makes a home.
screen: `TWO POLES AND A WIRE.` → `NO SIGN, NO POWER.` → `A STROLLER ON SHABBAT.`

segments.voice: Eruv. Start with yesterday's last father: carrying from one domain to another. Inside your own home you can carry on Shabbat. Out in the public domain, or from a private space into a public one, you can't. The rabbis tie that rule to the Torah's words, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "abide ye every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day." So a key, a book, a baby who can't walk yet: all of it stays inside. The rabbis didn't erase that rule. They asked a different question. What is a home? First, a home is shared food. In the Mishnah's tractate Eruvin, the families around a shared courtyard each put in some food, and it's kept together in one house. Now they're one household eating from one table, and the courtyard between them is no longer no one's space. It's theirs. Second, a home has doorways. The Talmud says that two posts with a crosspiece over them count as the form of a doorway. Run that doorway around a neighborhood, pole to pole, wire across the top, and the space inside can be treated as one enclosure. That's the wire in the hook. Third, a home has to be kept. Communities that rely on an eruv check it before Shabbat, because a broken wire can mean it doesn't hold that week. And not every Jewish community uses one. Some Orthodox authorities are strict about which eruvin they rely on, and Jews who don't keep the carrying rules have no need for one. Underneath the details is the rabbis' move. The law about staying in your place is honored, and the neighbors become one place. A string makes a home.
screen: `CARRYING STAYS INSIDE.` · `A HOME IS SHARED FOOD.` · `A HOME HAS DOORWAYS.` · `A HOME HAS TO BE KEPT.` · then, large: `A STRING MAKES A HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice. Sit, and let your breath slow. Picture the few homes closest to yours: the neighbors on either side, above, below, across. Names, if you know them. A face, if you don't. Now picture a thin line running around all of you, turning the street into one house. Who's inside it with you? Who would you bring a dish to? Later, if you're curious, find out whether your area has an eruv. Some communities post a map. The bell holds the time.
Eruv. A shared meal and a boundary of poles and wire that let a whole neighborhood count as one home for carrying on Shabbat. Today's word.
Your line: a string makes a home. Today, do one small thing that makes your street a little more shared: a greeting, a returned bin, a plate passed over the fence. Day one thousand seventy-three.

howItsDone: In some Jewish neighborhoods a community builds an eruv of poles and wire, checks it each week before Shabbat and announces whether it is up; families who rely on it then carry within it on Shabbat. Others who keep the carrying rules carry nothing outside without one.

fork.setup: you share a courtyard with three other families. on Shabbat you want to carry a dish from your door to your neighbor's. what do you do?
options: carry it anyway; it's only a few steps.
before Shabbat, all the families put food together in one house.

fork.reveal: the Mishnah's answer is shared food. pooled in one house, it makes the families one household, and the courtyard becomes theirs to carry in.

original.note: Hebrew: the arrangement that joins households or spaces into one for Shabbat.

trapdoor: what you thought: a loophole made of string.
what it means: a way of honoring the rule about carrying by making neighbors into one shared home.
what a scholar hears: tractate Eruvin in the order Moed, food pooled to join courtyards, and the Talmud's form of a doorway: two posts and a crosspiece.
